rules.name: Repeated syntactic frame
rules.description: Three or more consecutive sentences built on the same syntactic frame, with different words in the slots. The paper's own example is a run of “Dr. Smith, a researcher at Oxford University, found that…”. The `echo` detector cannot see this, because every content word differs; what repeats is the shape. Content words are wildcarded and only the closed class is compared, so the badge shows the frame that repeated.
rules.suggest: Vary the sentence shapes, or collapse the run into one sentence and a list. Three identical frames read as a form someone filled in.
rules.note: A crude stand-in for part-of-speech tagging, which this engine does not have. It found zero false positives in 30,300 words of human technical prose, but the guard doing most of that work is the requirement that a frame contain at least two closed-class anchors — without it, code and table rows match each other.

rules.name: Too few commas
rules.description: LLM prose uses fewer commas than human prose. The Economist compared 55,940 sentences of its own journalism, CNN, the New York Times, the Washington Post and novels from 1950 to 2022 against four models rewriting the same articles, and found the models short of commas, semicolons and parentheses alike.
rules.suggest: No single sentence is wrong. The document as a whole reads as a run of flat declaratives; vary the shapes.

After three failures the batch moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue every morning. Most entries turn out to be malformed input. They come from one upstream partner. We opened a ticket with them in March. The ticket is still open. We now reject their malformed records at the edge instead. That reduced the dead letter volume by ninety percent. The remaining failures are genuine bugs on our side. We fix them as they appear. The edge rejection was a fifteen line change. It shipped on a Tuesday afternoon. Nobody noticed it. rules.name: Sentences run long
rules.description: Fewer than 20 sentence endings per 1000 words is an average sentence of 50 words or more. Long sentences with few short ones among them were one of the Economist's confirmed markers, alongside sparse punctuation.
rules.suggest: Break the longest ones. A short sentence after a long one is what makes the long one readable.
